When you have a hard decision to make, it is really tempting to just ask one person you trust and then go with whatever they tell you. That is faster, and it feels safer because you only have to hear one answer. But most of the time, asking two or three people ends up being the better move, even though it takes longer and can be confusing at first.

The biggest reason is that every person you ask only knows part of the story. Last year I had to decide whether to keep doing band or switch to art for my elective. I asked my mom first and she said stay in band, because she had already paid for the clarinet rental and she thought quitting things looks bad. That is a real reason, but it is a mom reason. Then I asked my band teacher, who told me that eighth grade is when the music actually gets fun and that a lot of people quit right before the good part. That is also a real reason, but of course a band teacher is going to say that. Finally I asked my cousin who is a junior in high school, and she said nobody in high school cares what elective you took in middle school, so pick whichever one you will actually look forward to. Three people, three completely different angles, and none of them were lying. If I had only asked my mom I never would have known that the teacher and my cousin were both thinking about things she wasn't.

Another reason is that people have different amounts of experience with the thing you are deciding. If you are buying a used bike off of Facebook Marketplace, your friend can tell you if it looks cool, but your uncle who fixes bikes can tell you that the frame is bent and you should walk away. Doctors do this too. If a doctor says you need surgery, a lot of people go get a second opinion, and that is not because they think the first doctor is a bad person. It is because it is a big permanent decision and it is worth making sure two separate people who went to medical school agree.

Hearing more than one opinion also helps you figure out what you actually want. Sometimes somebody gives you advice and your stomach drops, and right then you realize you were hoping they would say the opposite. You would never find that out if you only asked one person and did what they said.

Of course, you can take this too far. If you ask fifteen people you will just get fifteen answers and be more stuck than when you started, and some people will just tell you what they think you want to hear. But asking a few people, especially people who are different from each other, gives you a fuller picture. In the end you still have to be the one who chooses. You just get to choose while actually knowing what you are choosing between.

A cousin who had the same surgery knows what nobody wrote down: that you cannot get up your own stairs for a while, that the sleeping is the worst part. None of these three is lying, and none of them is giving a complete picture. Put together, they describe a decision rather than a recommendation.

Multiple opinions also expose the parts of advice that are really just personality. Ask five people whether to lend a friend money and you will hear two who say never, under any circumstances, and two who say of course, that is what friends are for, and one who asks how much and whether you would still be friends if it were never paid back. That is when you start asking yourself what you actually want, which is the question you should have been asking the whole time. In a weird way, people disagreeing with each other is more helpful than everybody agreeing, because it hands the decision back to you.

You can even see this in things way bigger than middle school. Doctors do it all the time. If somebody gets told they need a serious surgery, almost everybody tells them to get a second opinion, and that is not because the first doctor is bad at their job. It is because the stakes are high and one person can miss something. Courts do it too. That is the whole point of having a jury of twelve people instead of one person deciding, because twelve people notice more than one person does and they have to talk it through.

I am not saying you should ask twenty people. If you ask everyone in your grade what to do, you will get twenty answers and end up more stuck than when you started, and you will probably just pick whichever one you liked hearing best anyway. There is also the problem that if you keep asking until someone agrees with you, you are not really getting advice, you are just shopping for permission. So there is a limit to it. But asking two or three people who actually know something about the situation, and who might not tell you the same thing, is almost always worth the extra time.

In the end I stayed on swim and did the spring play instead, which was not either of the options I started with. I only found that option because two people told me two different things and I had to sit down and think about it myself. That is what multiple opinions really do. They do not hand you the answer. They show you the parts of the choice you could not see on your own, and then you make a better decision because you are finally seeing the whole thing.

I asked my mom and she said do band because I already play trumpet and I've been doing it since 5th grade and it would be a waste to quit. That sounded right so I almost just did that. My mom didn't know that because she never went to school here. So one person gave me an opinion and the other person gave me a fact that changed the whole question. If I had only asked one, I would have picked without even knowing there was a third option.

If you ask one friend "does this sound mean" and they say no, you believe them, because what else do you have. It's like when you take your temperature with a thermometer that might be broken. One reading doesn't prove anything by itself. You need something to compare it to. My social studies teacher told us that when we research we need more than one source because a source can have a bias, and I think people are the same way. My friend who is on the team is going to tell me the team is great. Of course she is. She's not lying, but she only sees one side.

Sometimes you already know the answer and you just need to hear it out loud from a few people before you admit it.

Asking more than one person takes longer and sometimes it makes you more confused for a while, but you end up knowing more about your choice than you did before, and that is the whole point.

The first reason is that every person you ask only knows part of the story. Last year I had to pick between taking band or taking a computer class for my elective. I asked my older brother, and he said take band, it is easy and you get to go on trips. So I almost signed up right there. Then I mentioned it to my mom and she asked me if I actually wanted to practice an instrument for an hour every week at home, because that is what my brother did and he complained about it constantly. I had never even thought about the practicing part. My brother was not lying to me, he just told me the part he remembered liking. My mom remembered the part she had to nag him about. Neither one of them was wrong, they just each had one piece.

The second reason is that people have their own reasons for wanting you to choose something, even if they do not say it out loud. My friend Jenna wanted me to take band because she was taking band and she wanted somebody to sit with. That is not a bad reason to be her friend but it is a bad reason for me to pick an elective. When I asked more people, her opinion became just one opinion instead of the only opinion, and it stopped pulling me so hard. If you only ask one person you cannot tell the difference between good advice and advice that happens to be good for them.

Another thing is that when a bunch of different people all say the same thing, that actually means something. Doctors do this. If a doctor tells someone they need surgery, a lot of people go get a second opinion, and if the second doctor says the exact same thing, now the person can feel a lot more sure about a scary decision. But if the second doctor says there is a medicine you could try first, then the person just learned about an option they did not even know existed. Either way they are better off than they were, which is kind of the perfect example, because both possible answers help you.

I do think there is a limit. If you ask fifteen people you will get fifteen answers and then you will just be stuck and annoyed, and eventually you have to be the one who decides. My grandpa says advice is free and that is exactly what it is worth, which I think is his way of saying you still have to think for yourself at the end.

But that is different from only asking one person and calling it research. When you get a few opinions you find out what you did not know, you find out who has a reason to push you, and you find out if everybody agrees. I ended up taking the computer class and I am glad, but honestly the thing I would say I actually learned that year was to ask around before I sign anything.

But I think asking more than one person is usually the smarter move, because one person only knows what one person knows, and even if they are really smart, that is still not everything.

The biggest reason is that everybody gives advice out of their own life. Last spring I had to choose between track and the spring musical, since they both have practice after school and you cannot do both. I asked my older brother first. He ran track in high school and he told me track, no question, because you get in shape and colleges like sports. That sounded good until I asked my aunt, who was in theater, and she said the play would be better for me because I am shy and it would push me out of that. Neither of them was lying to me. They were both telling me what worked for them. If I had only asked my brother I would have thought there was only one right answer, when really there were two answers and they each had a reason behind them.

Another reason is that some people will just tell you what you want to hear. My friends do this constantly. If I ask my best friend whether my project idea is good, she is going to say yes, because she is my friend and she does not want me to feel bad. That is nice of her but it is not actually useful. When I asked my science teacher the same question, she said my idea was too big for the time we had and I should pick one part of it instead. That was not what I wanted to hear, but she was right, and my project turned out way better because I cut it down. If I had stopped after one opinion I would have had a mess.

Multiple opinions also help you see what everybody agrees on. When my parents were trying to figure out if my grandma needed a different medicine, they went to a second doctor. Both doctors said the same thing about one part of it, and that made my parents a lot more sure they were doing the right thing. When people who do not know each other land on the same answer, that answer is probably solid. And when they disagree, that tells you something too. It tells you this is a real choice with tradeoffs, not something obvious you are just too dumb to figure out.

I am not saying you should go ask fifty people, because then you would be so confused you would never decide anything. But asking two or three people who see the world differently gives you more information than asking one. In the end you are still the one who picks. You just pick knowing more.

When you have a hard choice to make, it is usually a bad idea to only ask one person. I think asking more than one person helps you make a better choice because everybody knows different stuff, everybody is biased in their own way, and hearing different answers makes you actually think about what you want instead of just doing what someone told you.

The first reason is that one person can only tell you what they know. Last year I wanted to do track and I asked my older cousin about it. She ran track in high school and she told me it was great and I should definitely do it. But she was a sprinter. I am not fast. If I had only listened to her I would have signed up thinking I was going to be running the 100 and then been really disappointed. I also asked my gym teacher and he said that I had good endurance from soccer and that I should try the longer distance stuff instead. That was information my cousin just did not have, not because she was wrong but because she only knew her own experience. Two people gave me two pieces of a picture and together it was a lot more useful than either one alone.

The second reason is that everybody has a bias, even when they are trying to help you. My mom's advice is almost always the safe option. If I ask her about anything she is going to tell me the thing that has the least chance of something going wrong. My friend Jalen is the opposite, he thinks everything sounds fun and you should just go for it. Neither of them is lying to me. They just see the world differently. If I only ask my mom I will never take a risk, and if I only ask Jalen I will do a lot of dumb things. When I ask both of them I can kind of see where the middle is. It is like how you are supposed to use more than one source when you write a research paper, because one website might have a slant to it and you will not notice the slant if you never read anything else.

Another thing is that when two people disagree, that actually tells you something. If you ask three people about a decision and all three say the same thing, that is a pretty strong sign. But if they all say something different, that is a sign that this is a closer call than you thought and you should slow down. In my science class we did an experiment and one group got a totally different result than everyone else, and instead of ignoring it my teacher made us figure out why. That is kind of what disagreement does with advice. It shows you the parts of the decision that are actually complicated instead of letting you think it is simple.

Also, and I think this is the part people forget, explaining your problem over and over helps you. Every time you tell somebody the situation you have to put it in words again, and sometimes by the third time you are saying it you already know what you want to do. My sister was trying to decide whether to quit her job and she asked like five people, and she said afterward that she pretty much decided while she was talking to the third one. The advice from the other two did not even matter that much. Just saying it out loud enough times made it clear.

Now I do think there is a limit. If you ask too many people you can get overwhelmed and end up more confused than when you started, and some people just keep asking until somebody finally tells them what they wanted to hear anyway. That is not really getting advice, that is shopping for permission. So you should ask people who actually know something about the thing and who will be honest with you even if it is not what you want.

But overall, asking more than one person is almost always better. You get information that one person could not have given you, you can see past their biases, disagreement shows you what is actually hard about the choice, and saying it out loud helps you figure out your own head. At the end the decision is still yours, but you are making it with a lot more to go on.
